core: What transportation geography studies: the movement of people, freight, and information across space, and how movement both shapes and is shaped by geography
The main modes of transport (road, rail, water/maritime, air, pipeline) and their trade-offs in cost, speed, and capacity
Transport networks described as nodes (hubs/terminals) and links (routes), with connectivity and accessibility
How transportation shapes settlement patterns, trade, and land value
Time-space convergence: places grow closer in travel time as transport improves
Containerization (from the mid-1950s) and its transformative effect on global shipping and trade

claims.claim: Transport geography is a sub-discipline concerned with the mobility of people, freight, and information, and studies how transportation both shapes and is shaped by geography.

There are five principal modes of transport (road, rail, water/maritime, air, pipeline), and competition among them depends chiefly on distance, the quantity shipped, and the value of what is carried; maritime moves the largest volumes over long distances at the lowest variable cost, road is most competitive over short distances and small loads, air is fastest and most expensive and suits high-value time-sensitive freight, and rail offers high overland capacity for bulk goods.

A transport network is a framework of routes among locations, where nodes are the locations (terminals, hubs, ports, airports) and links are the routes between them; the relevance of a network relates to its connectivity, and a location's accessibility reflects how easily it can be reached from other nodes.

Time-space convergence describes the reduction in travel time between places as transport technology improves, making places effectively 'closer'; the concept was formalized by geographer Donald Janelle in the late 1960s, illustrated by the fall in Edinburgh-to-London travel time from a multi-day stagecoach journey to a flight of about two hours.

Container shipping began with the voyage of the Ideal-X, which departed Newark, New Jersey, on April 26, 1956, and reached Houston, Texas, five days later carrying 58 truck-body containers; the venture was led by trucking entrepreneur Malcolm McLean.

Containerization sharply cut cargo-handling costs: loading a medium-sized ship the conventional break-bulk way was estimated at about $5.83 per ton in 1956, while loading standardized containers cost under $0.16 per ton, and containers that once took days to load by hand could be loaded in hours.

The International Organization for Standardization set worldwide container dimensions during discussions beginning in the late 1950s (a standard 40-foot length among them), and this interchangeability let boxes move seamlessly among ships, trucks, and trains, helping reorganize global trade.
Accessibility within a network is associated with better opportunities, so transport networks influence which locations develop and prosper, shaping settlement, trade, and land value.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The conventional-loading cost figure and McLean's birth year vary slightly among sources.
positions: The Geography of Transport Systems gives $5.83 per ton and McLean's dates as 1914-2001.
Some secondary retellings give $5.86 per ton; Smithsonian Magazine gives McLean's birth as 1913.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Used the OER figure ($5.83 per ton) and attributed it; framed the cost as approximate. Avoided asserting a precise birth year, describing McLean simply as a trucking entrepreneur active in the 1950s. The one-day-loading-in-hours-versus-days and the sub-$0.16-per-ton figures are consistent across sources.

sourceRecords.title: The First Containership, Ideal-X, 1956 (The Geography of Transport Systems)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. Supports the dated containerization facts: the Ideal-X departed Newark, NJ on April 26, 1956, and reached Houston, TX five days later carrying 58 35-foot (8x8 ft) containers plus bulk petroleum; Malcolm McLean was a trucking entrepreneur whose 1937 experience of slow break-bulk loading motivated the idea; conventional loading was about $5.83 per ton versus under $0.16 per ton for containers; boxes loaded in under eight hours; McLean founded Sea-Land (1960), later acquired by Maersk (1999). Same educational-use-only terms as the parent site; REFERENCE_ONLY, no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: The Now-Ubiquitous Shipping Container Was an Idea Before Its Time
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. Independent corroboration of the April 26, 1956 Ideal-X voyage (Newark to Houston, 58 container bodies) and Malcolm McLean's background (founded McLean Trucking 1934, sold it 1955 to enter shipping, founded Sea-Land, died 2001). Supports the labor impact (containerization displaced dockworker jobs; unions struck before early-1960s displacement-payment agreements), ISO standardization discussions beginning 1958 (including a standard 40-foot length, with McLean allowing royalty-free use of Sea-Land corner-fitting patents), and the growth of container trade. Copyrighted; REFERENCE_ONLY, facts synthesized and rewritten.
